items.title: Z.ai runs GLM inference on 100,000 Chinese AI chips, eyes overseas CSPs
items.summary_1line: Z.ai runs GLM inference on 100,000 Chinese AI chips, eyes overseas CSPs digitimes
items.editor_note: digitimes reports the GLM inference build now runs on 100,000 Chinese chips, with Z.ai eyeing overseas cloud service providers next.

editorial.tldr: Z.ai's CEO framed GLM 5.3 around a new post-training scaling law and an early hands-on review covered its pricing, but the release itself was delayed days later over disclosed cybersecurity risks.
editorial.whats_new: Z.ai's underlying GLM inference build now spans 100,000 domestic Chinese AI chips, with the company reportedly in talks to bring it to overseas cloud providers.
editorial.why_it_matters: GLM 5.3's economics are tied to a domestic-chip inference path; teams evaluating it should hold off assuming Western-GPU parity or overseas availability until Z.ai names specific providers.
editorial.take_for_builders: Hold off deploying GLM 5.3 assuming Western-GPU parity — once Z.ai names its overseas cloud providers, confirm whether that hosting still runs on the same domestic-chip inference path before committing.

status.state: Delayed, now scaling on domestic chips
status.reenable: no fixed release date or named overseas provider yet
status.detail: GLM 5.3's release slipped past its expected date after a disclosed cybersecurity risk; the inference build behind it has since scaled to 100,000 domestic chips, with Z.ai reportedly courting overseas cloud providers to host it.

open_questions: What cybersecurity risk triggered the Aug 22 delay, and has Z.ai confirmed a fix or a firm release date?
Which overseas cloud providers is Z.ai in talks with, and would hosting there still depend on domestic-chip supply?
Does the post-training scaling law CEO Jie Tang described apply to the model now running on 100,000 chips, or is that a separate infrastructure track?
